newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Search still on for Mobutu-Kabila talks venue.
newsitem.headline: Search still on for Mobutu-Kabila talks venue.

text.p: Zaire's veteran president, Mobutu Sese Seko, is still prepared to meet rebel leader Laurent Kabila for face-to-face talks but the question remains where, Mobutu's son and spokesman said on Wednesday.
Nzanga Mobutu told a news conference in the capital Kinshasa that his father had declined on health grounds an invitation from President Nelson Mandela to travel to South Africa for the talks.
He said Kabila, in turn, had rejected Congo's capital Brazzaville as an alternative venue and had instead proposed Zaire's rebel-held second city of Lubumbashi.
"Mobutu is still agreed to the principle of talks. It's only a question of the venue," he said.

Nzanga Mobutu, who sidestepped a question on whether Mobutu would go to Lubumbashi, said his father had told Mandela in a telephone call on Tuesday that he could not travel to South Africa for the talks.
"He's not too sick. He is still convalescing," Nzanga told the news conference.
Mobutu had prostate cancer in Europe last August.

Nzanga Mobutu said Kabila, whose forces took up arms in October and control half of Zaire, had turned down an offer from President Pascal Lissouba of Congo that the talks take place in his capital Brazzaville -- just across the river from Kinshasa.
"Kabila said he would not go to Congo but proposed the city of Lubumbashi," he added.
Asked whether Mobutu would go to Lubumbashi, he replied: "That is what Kabila proposed to Mandela. In a few days time, we will know more."

Asked whether the choice of Lubumbashi was provocative, Nzanga Mobutu replied: "Provocative, no, but this is not a neutral zone. South Africa is a neutral zone, Congo is a neutral zone, Lubumbashi is not."
Kabila and his forces say Zaire's teeming capital Kinshasa is their final major target. Nzanga Mobutu played down rebel talk of an early attack on the city.
"He's always talking," he said of Kabila, but he added: "We cannot allow bloodshed in Kinshasa."
